title: Microsoft Fluent Acrylic material
lede: Microsoft’s frosted-glass brush for Windows apps: blur, tint, and noise over the desktop, three years before the style had a name.
summary: Fluent Design’s translucent Acrylic brush and its documented recipe. Microsoft, 2017 onward.
made: 2017 (Fluent Design System; first shipped in the Windows 10 Fall Creators Update, October 2017, per Wikipedia); documentation page updated 2026

evidence.note: Read the documentation page (ms.date 2026-08-29) and inspected two of its images in scratchpad copies: the Windows 11 context menu over a colorful wallpaper (acrylic-transient-context-menu.png, 1591 × 871) and the recipe diagram (acrylic-recipe-diagram.jpg, 1920 × 1080). Not stored.

styles.note: NN/g and t3n name Acrylic as glassmorphism under another name, and Malewicz quotes it in the naming article. It is the style’s material in a shipping design system.

context: The page defines Acrylic as “a type of Brush that creates a translucent texture” that adds depth and helps establish visual hierarchy. Background acrylic shows the desktop and other windows; in-app acrylic shows content inside the app. [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/style/acrylic).

Guidance: use background acrylic for transient surfaces such as context menus and flyouts; avoid layering several acrylic surfaces and placing acrylic panes edge to edge; do not place accent-colored text on acrylic. Acrylic falls back to a solid color when the user turns off transparency effects, in Battery Saver mode, in High Contrast mode, and on low-end hardware.

The text gives the recipe as “background, blur, exclusion blend, color/tint overlay, noise”. The diagram labels the layers Desktop background, Gaussian blur, Luminosity blend, Tint/Color blend, and Noise texture; the two labels for the blend layer differ.

Fluent Design (codename Project Neon) was introduced by Microsoft in 2017 with five components: light, depth, motion, material, and scale. [Wikipedia: Fluent Design System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluent_Design_System). Microsoft’s [materials overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/apps/design/signature-experiences/materials) calls Acrylic “a semi-transparent material that replicates the effect of frosted glass”.
observed: Context-menu screenshot: a File Explorer window sits on a wallpaper of blurred violet, magenta, red, blue, and cyan light.
The context menu is a pale, pink-tinted translucent panel. The wallpaper colors show through it as soft washes, with no detail.
The menu has rounded corners, a thin light edge, and a soft shadow. Its icons and text are dark and flat.
Recipe diagram: five slanted sheets in a stack, from a saturated blue ‘desktop’ through a blurred sheet, a grey blend sheet, a light-blue tint, and a grey noise texture.
interpretation: Acrylic is the style before its name, fixed as an engineering recipe. The noise layer is Microsoft’s addition; web glassmorphism usually leaves it out.
borrow: Add a faint noise texture over the blur and tint so that large glass areas do not look like a plain gradient.
Give every glass surface a solid fallback for reduced-transparency settings.
